A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WeightWatch research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and Appendix F report original detection, steering, and model-auditing results.

after.justification: Sections 5–6 and Appendices D–G retain original empirical results and add FFT checkpoint evaluations and an MTBA replication.

M1.justification: The weight-difference SVD, cosine-range monitoring, and activation-orthogonalization steering procedures remain unchanged. The k=20 setting emphasized in v2 already appears in v1's Algorithm 1. Revised backdoor training concerns evaluated models, not the proposed monitoring method.

E1.justification: The case study drops the noisy WildChat real-life scenario, retaining the matched harmful/benign setup; WildChat remains in calibration and auditing experiments. FFT training also replaces BackdoorLLM-based data with StrongREJECT and UltraChat examples. The broader backdoor, unlearning, and multilingual auditing tasks remain.

E2.justification: PCA, natural-language probes, KL divergence, activation-difference norm, and BEAT remain comparison methods. The circuit-breaker attack comparisons are also retained. Moving KL discussion into Appendix G.1 does not remove that baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix D.2 substantially revises FFT preparation: three epochs and batch size 4 become five epochs and batch size 8, with newly constructed Gemma-generated training responses and partial-trigger negatives for CTBA. V2 evaluates checkpoints at steps 100–500 and additional trigger variants. The limited-data PCA setting also changes from 3 to 10 triggered examples.

E4.justification: V2 adds an MTBA trigger-replacement diagnostic addressing the suspected effect of common trigger words in calibration data (Appendix D.4). It removes the real-life PCA, probing, and KL case-study analyses. Existing weight-subtraction and unlearning-steering analyses remain.

E5.justification: V1 reports individual model values; v2 introduces checkpoint averages and contribution counts, with raw results in Table 7. FFT averages use five checkpoints from one badnet model and fifteen from three models for each of CTBA and MTBA. These are checkpoint/trigger-variant aggregates, not fifteen independent seeded runs. No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or seed values are added.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces FFT completion-flagging results of 100.00%, 44.44%, and 74.75% with averages of 98.59%, 56.43%, and 72.59% under revised training and aggregation. New Tables 7–8 report checkpoint variability and MTBA replication results, including 52.53% prompt and 69.70% completion flagging. Figure 8 also changes KL values, such as benign-to-harmful divergence from 4.20 to 4.13, and removes real-life entries. Individual PPO, unlearning, and auditing results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, false-positive argument, and rank-one update derivation remain substantively unchanged. V2 shortens the main false-positive bound to its existing asymptotic expression, while Appendix A retains the fuller expression and the same proof.

C1.justification: The backdoor headline changes from 13 individual models with 44–100% completion flagging to nine aggregated setups with 56–100%, and the reported FPR limit changes from 1.20% to 1.04%. The specific claim of completely neutralizing attacks in nine of thirteen models disappears. The central monitoring, unlearning-recovery, and auditing contributions remain.

C2.justification: Section 6 explicitly limits open-ended auditing to behaviors represented in calibration transcripts. Appendix E also suggests that WHP's steering resistance reflects more fundamental, belief-level changes from SFT, extending v1's description of resistant incorrect beliefs. Existing limitations concerning adversarial robustness and base-weight access remain.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds or revises actionable FFT data-construction details, response-generator identities, checkpoint steps, and trigger strings. It specifies batch size 16 for the MTBA replication and acknowledges uncertainty about the original batch size. A project-page address is added; the existing precision, calibration, clustering, and prompt documentation is retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gur-Arieh et al. (2025), Hong et al. (2024), and the Gemma 3 technical report, while removing Perin et al. (2025) on LoX. It modestly expands unlearning context and makes its relationship to task arithmetic and prior weight analysis more explicit.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and compresses the introduction, background, case study, and experiment narrative. Unlearning auditing joins the reorganized Section 6, detailed steering moves to Appendix E, and related work moves after the references. A conclusion and LLM contribution statement are added.

P2.justification: V2 changes typography, headers, and reference styling; redraws the overview and case-study graphics; and reduces the PCA, probing, and KL displays. It restructures the setup table, introduces aggregate and raw-result displays, and relocates the pseudocode and steering figures and tables.

improvement.justification: V2 improves reproducibility and auditability through clearer FFT data construction, partial-trigger controls, and checkpoint-level reporting, while better distinguishing controlled detection from calibration-limited auditing. These are useful but limited gains. Noisy real-life case-study evidence is lost, and the new averages include checkpoints before the stated backdoor-implantation stage (Appendix D.3), limiting their support for stronger robustness claims.
